text.p: French appliance maker Moulinex is on track to recover its competitive edge after the first year of a tough restructuring programme, but success is not guaranteed, chairman Pierre Blayau said on Wednesday.
"This is a convalescing company where we are implementing profound changes," he told Reuters in an interview on the 1996/97 results which marked the first annual profit since 1991.

"There's nothing in the full-year results or assessment of the measures taken that allows us to say success is guaranteed. But the results and achievements of the past year allow us to say we're on track. I'm sure it's doable," he said.
The company provoked a storm of protest from union leaders and politicians last year when it announced the plan entailing 2,600 job cuts, nearly a quarter of the staff, and two plant closures.
Although the restructuring pales next to a plan announced by Electrolux to shut 25 plants and shed 12,000 jobs, Moulinex's staff cuts were propotionately deeper.
After months of tension and negotiations, Moulinex reduced the number of planned staff cuts in France to 1,350 from 2,100 by shortening work schedules at its French plants.

Close to 1,000 French employees have left under early retirement or other schemes. "Given the objective of 1,350 departures, it shows the plan is far along," Blayau said. The two plants slated for closure will be shut in July.

Blayau said he had not amended the targets set last year when, shortly after his arrival, he announced the restructuring plan designed to bring Moulinex's competitiveness in line with that of its rivals.

The goals were to increase operating profit to eight percent of sales by cutting staff, purchasing and logistical costs, generate sales of nine billion francs, up from 7.7 billion in the year ended on March 31, and boost sales per worker to one million francs from 700,000.

On Wednesday Moulinex reported a 29 million franc net attributable profit for 1996/97, compared with a 702 million loss for 1995/96 that included a 600 million restructuring charge. Operating profit jumped to 160 million francs from 54 million, representing about two percent of turnover.
Blayau declined to quantify the progress on other targets. "The proof of the pudding will be the 1998/99 results," he said.
But he predicted a significant rise in operating profit and return on capital for 1997/98, even if consumer spending remains sluggish in Europe.
He also said that, in a bid to lift morale at the "traumatised" company, he planned to propose negotiations in September to establish a profit-sharing plan for employees.
Blayau said market conditions remain difficult, with little sign of sales recovery in France or western Europe overall, but no new restructuring charges are envisaged for the current year.
The company, which also owns the Krups brand of coffee-makers, hopes to make up for the slow growth in Europe by expanding into new markets.
"We're too dependent on Europe. We need to accelerate international expansion," he said, recalling the recent signing of a joint venture in China.
The group is also stepping up product launches, putting out 130 new or revamped appliances between now and December, a 30 percent increase over the launches in June-December 1996.
About 20 of the new products are in the growing personal care segment, such as electric toothbrushes.
